To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the F1 hybrids between BALB/c and SENCAR mice developed both persistent epidermal proliferation and skin tumors, whereas the F1 hybrids from the C57BL6 X SENCAR cross did not develop either of these two characteristics.

susceptibility to phototumor development is completely recessive in F1 hybrids from SENCAR x C57BL/ 6 mice, but is incompletely recessive (partially dominant) in F1 hybrids derived from SENCAR and the more UV-resistant strain, BALB/c mice.
the susceptibility to persistent hyperplasia is a necessary, but not sufficient, requirement for susceptibility to skin tumors in SENCAR mice.

identifying the genetic and molecular mechanisms that control the response of the epidermis to UV radiation-induced damage.
understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying the induction of persistent epidermal proliferation and skin tumorigenesis by UV irradiation, using SENCAR mice as an animal model.
understanding the genetic basis of susceptibility to UV radiation-induced skin carcinogenesis.

susceptibility to phototumor induction in the F1 hybrids is determined by a single autosomal locus, with the C57BL allele being dominant over the BALB allele, but recessive to the SENCAR allele.

susceptibility to both persistent hyperplastic epidermal hyperreactivity and phototumorigenicity is inherited as a single, incompletely recessive trait in mice.

the susceptibility to phototumor development in SENCAR mice is controlled by a single gene, which has a dominant effect on susceptibility to phototomorigenesis, a recessive effect on susceptibility to persistent hyperplasia, and an intermediate effect on the development of both characteristics in F1 hybrids with the resistant BALB/c strain.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the SENCAR mouse model for UV-induced skin cancer is genetically complex, and that the genetic factors involved in the susceptibility to persistent hyperplasia are distinct from those involved in the susceptibility of phototumorigenic response.
susceptibility to phototumor formation is not a simple, binary trait.
